phonemes.desc: Syllable beginning with labio-velar glide [w], high back rounded vowel [u], and Tone 3 (falling-rising, ˨˩˦). In connected speech before a non-third tone, this is often realized as a 'half-third' low falling tone.
Syllable with voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative [ɕ], high front vowel [i], velar nasal [ŋ], and Tone 2 (rising, ˧˥). Pinyin 'x' before front vowels is always [ɕ], like an extended 'sh' in 'she'.

pronunciation.approximation: WOO-SHING — 'wu' dips low and rises (or stays low in fast speech), and 'xing' rises like 'sheen' with a rising tone.

kin.form: 金木水火土 jīn-mù-shuǐ-huǒ-tǔ (metal, wood, water, fire, earth)

pronunciation.note: 五行 (Wǔxíng) denotes the 'Five Phases' or 'Five Agents'—wood, fire, earth, metal, and water—the cyclical modes of transformation in Chinese cosmology, medicine, and feng shui. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading in this philosophical context is wǔ (Tone 3) + xíng (Tone 2), as given by the Unihan Database (kMandarin) and the Hanyu Pinyin scheme. Baxter & Sagart (2014) reconstruct 五 as *C.ŋˤaʔ (GSR 0058a) and 行 in the sense 'walk, conduct' as *C.[g]raŋ (GSR 0748a). The Unicode restoration Wǔxíng preserves the citation tones; note that 行 is disyllabically distinguished from the reading háng ('row, profession').

domains.title: The Five Phases
domains.subtitle: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water
domains.lead:
Wǔxíng is often mistranslated as 'five elements,' but xíng means movement, conduct, or phase. Wood, fire, earth, metal, and water are not static substances but dynamic processes: wood grows, fire flames, earth ripens, metal contracts, water descends. Together they form a grammar of transformation that Chinese thinkers applied to seasons, organs, emotions, dynasties, and military strategy.

The system works through two main cycles: the generating cycle (wood feeds fire, fire makes earth, earth bears metal, metal carries water, water nourishes wood) and the controlling cycle (wood parts earth, earth absorbs water, water quenches fire, fire melts metal, metal chops wood).

cards.name: Generation Cycle
cards.desc: Each phase gives birth to the next in a circle of mutual nourishment and support.

cards.name: Control Cycle
cards.desc: Each phase checks another, preventing any one process from running to destructive excess.

cards.name: Correspondence System
cards.desc: Every phase maps to a direction, season, color, organ, emotion, taste, and musical note.

cards.name: Cosmic Calendar
cards.desc: The phases organize the year: wood/spring, fire/summer, earth/late summer, metal/autumn, water/winter.

symbols.name: Wood
symbols.meaning: Growth, spring, the east, the liver, the color green/blue, the wind

symbols.name: Fire

symbols.name: Earth

symbols.name: Water

mythology.lead: Wǔxíng has no divine biography — it is a cosmology, not a theogony — but its intellectual history is dramatic. It began as a description of natural processes in the Shangshu, became a theory of dynastic legitimacy under Zou Yan, and ended as the diagnostic grammar of Traditional Chinese Medicine, where it still orders diagnosis today.

myths.title: The Great Plan
myths.text: The Hongfan ('Great Plan') chapter of the Shangshu presents the five materials as the first of the Nine Categories revealed to Yu the Great — the cosmic charter through which Heaven's order was transmitted to the founder of the Xia. Water, fire, wood, metal, and earth are listed with their natures: water soaks and descends, fire blazes and ascends, wood bends and straightens, metal yields and can be changed, earth receives sowing and yields harvests (Shangshu, Hongfan). This is the earliest systematic statement of Wǔxíng cosmology, and its setting matters as much as its content: the phases are handed down in the same breath as the laws of government, because in early Chinese thought there was no separating how nature behaves from how rule must behave. The myth's core meaning is that transformation is lawful — and law, understood deeply enough, is a description of transformation.

myths.title: The Yin-Yang and Five Phases School
myths.text: The philosopher Zou Yan (c. 305–240 BCE) of Qi turned the five phases into an engine of history. Sima Qian, who appends his biography to those of Mencius and Xunzi in the Shiji (ch. 74), records the doctrine: each dynasty rules by the virtue of one phase, and Heaven signals the coming transfer with omens — the Yellow Emperor possessed the virtue of earth, the Xia of wood, the Shang of metal, the Zhou of fire — so that each new house commands the phase that conquers its predecessor's. Conquest, not election, is the mechanism of legitimacy: the Qin claimed water (and the color black) to douse Zhou fire, and two centuries of Han debate argued whether the Han ruled by earth or by fire. Xunzi's school dismissed Zou Yan's talk of heaven as grandiose, but the emperors kept the theory for a simple reason — it made revolution look like meteorology. The myth means that cosmic legitimacy is a technology: whoever reads the phases correctly can crown a conquest as a season.

myths.title: Five Phases as Cosmic Seasons
myths.text: The Huainanzi, compiled at the court of Liu An around 139 BCE, integrates Wǔxíng with astronomy, music, and politics into a single encyclopedic vision. Its early chapters map the phases onto the heavens and the calendar: wood commands the east and the spring equinox, fire the south and the summer solstice, metal the west and the autumn, water the north and the winter — while earth holds the center and the season between. Each direction carries its emblems (the Green Dragon, the Red Bird, the White Tiger, the Dark Warrior), its pitch-pipe, its winds, its prohibitions, and the work of the month (Huainanzi, ch. 3–5). The text shows the system at its most ambitious: one grid in which the emperor's conduct, the farmer's calendar, and the music master's pitch pipes are different cells of the same pattern. The myth's meaning is the encyclopedia itself — correlative thinking as an attempt to live inside a cosmos where microcosm and macrocosm rhyme.

myths.title: The Body as Landscape
myths.text: The Huangdi Neijing ('Inner Classic of the Yellow Emperor') turns Wǔxíng into medicine. The liver belongs to wood, the heart to fire, the spleen to earth, the lungs to metal, and the kidneys to water — and with the organs come their whole retinue of correspondences: the eyes and sinews of wood, the tongue and vessels of fire, the mouth and flesh of earth, the nose and skin of metal, the ears and bones of water (Huangdi Neijing, Suwen). Health is the smooth circulation of these phases through their generating and controlling cycles; disease is their obstruction, rebellion, or excess — wood overacting on earth, fire failing to warm water. Diagnosis reads the five colors on the face, the five notes of the voice, and the five flavors of the patient's craving; treatment works through the same grammar, nourishing a mother phase to strengthen its child. The myth means that the body is not a machine with parts but a landscape with seasons — and the physician's art is the art of reading weather.

lore.syncretism: Wǔxíng was sometimes compared by Western observers to the Greek four elements, but the comparison is misleading. The Greek elements are building blocks of substance; the Chinese phases are patterns of change. A closer Indian analogue is the pañca mahābhūta, though the correspondences differ. Wǔxíng entered Japan as gogyō and Korea as ohaeng, shaping East Asian medicine, astrology, and martial arts. In modern times, Wǔxíng has been invoked — and sometimes distorted — in management theory, martial-arts branding, and popular spirituality, often reduced to a color-coded personality test. The medical tradition, however, continues to use the five phases as a sophisticated heuristic for pattern differentiation.
lore.culturalLegacy: Wǔxíng is the hidden scaffolding of much that looks merely 'Chinese' on the surface. The five flavors, five colors, five notes, five grains, and five directions all derive from it. Traditional Chinese Medicine diagnoses in its terms; feng shui designs spaces by it; Xingyiquan organizes its five basic fists around it; Chinese astrology assigns each year an element. The system even colored imperial ritual: the Yellow Emperor claimed earth, the Qin chose black water to overcome Zhou red fire. Today Wǔxíng survives in video-game elemental mechanics, wellness branding, and martial-arts school names — sometimes faithfully, often trivially. Its deepest legacy is a habit of mind: the tendency to see nature not as a collection of things but as a field of interactive processes.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Wǔxíng teaches that nothing is only what it is. Wood is also the process of becoming fire; fire is also the ash that becomes earth; earth is also the ore that becomes metal; metal is also the condensation that becomes water; water is also the nourishment that becomes wood. Identity, in this system, is a verb.

This has practical consequences. To treat a symptom in Chinese medicine is not to kill a germ but to rebalance a process. To choose an auspicious date is not to appease a god but to align with seasonal momentum. To practice Xingyiquan is to embody the five phases until they move through the body the way they move through the year. Wǔxíng is less a belief than a method: look for the pattern of change, and work with it rather than against it.

lore.archaeology: The textual foundation of Wǔxíng appears in the Shangshu's Hongfan chapter, transmitted through Warring States and Han manuscript traditions. The Mawangdui tomb library (sealed 168 BCE, excavated 1973) preserves early medical manuscripts that apply the five phases to diagnosis and treatment, while the Huangdi Neijing became the canonical medical synthesis. Han dynasty lacquerware, bronze mirrors, and tomb murals display the color-direction correspondences of the five phases. Unlike a deity, Wǔxíng has no temple, but its logic is inscribed across the material culture of state ritual, medicine, and calendrical science.
lore.originalScriptNote: The original script is 五行; traditional and simplified forms are identical. The Modern Standard Mandarin reading in the philosophical sense is Wǔxíng (Tone 3 + Tone 2), per Hanyu Pinyin and the Unihan Database. Note that 行 has a separate reading háng ('row, profession'); here it means 'movement, conduct, phase.' The registrable form preserves the tone marks; the characters are displayed in the Original Script card. Baxter & Sagart reconstruct 五 as *C.ŋˤaʔ and 行 in the sense 'walk, conduct' as *C.[g]raŋ.
